hazards: Crevasses on the Southwest Glacier, including a marginal snow bridge that persists in most seasons
Loose, sharp rock on the final Class 2-3/3-4 gullies, chimneys, and ribs near the summit
Slick, spray-soaked rock at the Depot Creek Falls crossing, aided by aging fixed hand-lines
Devil's club and slide alder brush hiding uneven footing on the lower approach
Extreme remoteness and lack of cell coverage complicating any self-rescue or evacuation
before.overview: Mount Spickard is a massive, heavily glaciated peak straddling the Skagit/Fraser drainage divide just 2 miles south of the Canadian border, part of the Chilliwack Group of the Skagit Range. It is the 5th-highest summit in North Cascades National Park and the 16th-highest in Washington, and its roughly 4,779 ft of prominence ranks 9th-greatest in the state. The mountain is built of Tertiary-age gneiss; the Silver Glacier drains north over a mile to Silver Lake, while a separate glacier system on the southwest side extends over 3 miles toward Mount Redoubt. First ascent is credited to Walter B. Reaburn in 1904; the peak's current name was applied in 1963 for climber Warren J. Spickard Jr., who died climbing a nearby peak in 1961. The standard Southwest Route/Silver Lake line climbs broad talus and a southwest glacier to a final short but loose Class 3-4 rock scramble, and is notable as much for its remote, cross-border approach as for its technical difficulty.
before.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel and steep snow, then exposed Class 3-4 scrambling to the summit; minimal rock pro.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - multi-day, off-trail approach up the Depot Creek/Silver Lake drainage with significant elevation gain before the summit day itself
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Moderate-heavy, roughly 35-45 lb for an overnight/multi-day approach carrying camping, glacier, and rock gear

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - typically a 2-3 day approach into the basin below the peak before a summit push; round trip is often a 3-4 day outing
requiredSkills: Cramponing and self-arrest on sustained 40-degree snow
Judgment for committing, hard-to-bail terrain given the long approach
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climber comfortable with glacier travel and exposed 3rd/4th class rock in remote, trail-less terrain near the international border; not a beginner objective

weather.typical: Cool, changeable North Cascades alpine weather; the best-season note to climb mid-summer through early fall reflects the need to avoid lingering early-season or accumulating late-season snow
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a hazard here - plan for early starts and being off exposed ridges and the glacier by early afternoon

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained, high-consequence terrain: a long, committing off-trail approach near the Canadian border, a glacier crossing, and exposed Class 3-4 rock to the summit. A fall or injury anywhere on this route means a slow, remote rescue.

avalanche.zone: North Cascades / Chilliwack border region - not covered by a specific NWAC forecast zone in season; NWAC issues forecasts only Nov-Apr for winter backcountry travel, so no avalanche advisory applies to this Jul-Sep glacier climbing window

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Short but genuine glacier crossing below the south ridge notch, with crevasse-fall hazard. Bridges are less consolidated early season and more open (but more visible) late season; carry rope and rescue gear even though some parties travel this short section unroped when bridges look solid.

access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the eleven named cross-country zones — Boston Basin, Eldorado, Forbidden, Hidden Lake, Icy, Inspiration, Nooksack, Price, Sulphide Glacier, Torment Basin and Triad — one of which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit, quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center up to a day ahead.

pitch_detail.notes: Ascend Torment's South Ridge (or SE Face) on loose 4th/low-5th terrain to a grassy ledge and V-shaped notch below the summit; leave packs, tag the summit, and downclimb back to the notch.
An overhanging rappel on fixed slings from the notch drops onto the Forbidden Glacier.
Cross the Forbidden Glacier past bergschrunds, moats, and snow bridges to a saddle below Forbidden's north side; the route's most serious and season-dependent hazard.
Follow the exposed 'Sidewalk in the Sky' ridge crest, bypassing two gendarmes (first on the left, second on the right), to the West Ridge Notch.
Join Forbidden Peak's classic West Ridge (Fifty Classic Climbs route): 4th-class scrambling with a crux 5.6 tower pitch near the summit.
Descend the West Ridge (partial downclimb, ~1 rappel) then roughly 7 rappels down the Cat Scratch Gullies back toward Boston Basin.
Climb an open book angling left off the notch that starts the ridge, turning right at its top to a ledge, then a short second open book gains the crest.
Surmount a steeper tower via sloping, exposed ledges beneath a steep face; protection is sparse here.
Weave among towers on the exposed crest, continuing leftward on the southwest face.
Sustained low-5th and 4th-class climbing on good granite finishes the ridge to the summit; many parties simul-climb this last stretch.
